summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex history of sclerosing mesenteritis, chronic gastrointestinal dysmotility, and multiple prior bowel surgeries was admitted for acute abdominal pain, nausea, and inability to tolerate oral intake. Imaging confirmed a partial small bowel obstruction, managed conservatively with NPO status, intravenous hydration, and gastrointestinal decompression via her G-tube. She initially received hydromorphone via PCA for pain, but this was changed to as-needed morphine due to concerns for narcotic-induced ileus and worsening aphasia and somnolence. Neurology consultation attributed her neurological symptoms to psychiatric and chronic factors, as they improved with distraction and resolved with medication adjustment. Her bowel function gradually improved, with return of flatus and bowel movements, allowing advancement to a regular diet. A detached G-tube clip was noted to be freely migrating in the bowel but was not causing obstruction. She remained hemodynamically stable throughout, with no signs of infection or bleeding. By discharge, she was tolerating oral intake, ambulating independently, and back to her baseline pain and function. She was discharged home with follow-up plans, instructions to continue home medications including enoxaparin, and guidance on diet, activity, and warning signs.
